This technique is called \"paradoxical intention.\" Instead of trying to calm down, you\'re going to try to make yourself MORE anxious. As anxious as humanly possible.\n\nWhen you try to scare yourself even worse on purpose, your brain almost always goes \"Wait... this is ridiculous\" and the panic collapses.
In your imagination, stand up. See yourself unbuckling your seatbelt. People are looking at you. Really imagine the eyes on you.
Now walk to the front of the plane in your imagination. Your anxiety is visible. You\'re shaking. Make it dramatic.
Imagine grabbing the PA microphone. Every passenger can hear you now.
Say your worst fears out loud through that microphone. \"EVERYONE, LISTEN TO ME! This plane is going to crash! We\'re all going to die!\" Really commit to this absurdity.
Double down. \"See that flight attendant\'s face?! They KNOW we\'re doomed!\" Imagine trying to convince the entire plane to panic with you.
Now stop. Take a breath. If you really committed, the whole thing became so ridiculous that your anxiety broke and turned into humor.
You cannot voluntarily create a panic attack. When you try to panic harder, the mechanism breaks.
Anxiety thrives on feeling out of control. When you try to make it worse, you prove you ARE in control.
What if, instead of fighting, you invited the anxiety in? This technique gives you the power to stop taking it so seriously.
Next time you feel anxiety: \"Oh, you want me to panic? Okay, let\'s REALLY panic. Come on, anxiety, show me what you\'ve got.\"
Acceptance is not about liking the feeling; it\'s about stopping the war against it. When you stop fighting, you stop adding fuel to the fire.
Take a deep breath. Notice the anxiety as if it were a physical object. What color is it? What shape? Is it heavy or light?
Say to yourself: \"I don\'t like this feeling, but I can allow it to be here. I am willing to feel this right now.\"
Imagine you are a large, open space—like a massive hall—and the anxiety is just a small guest passing through. You are big enough to hold this feeling without it overwhelming you.
Breathe into the sensation. Instead of tightening around it, soften. Let the edges of the feeling become blurry.
Remind yourself: \"This is just a temporary visitor. It doesn\'t define me. I am the observer, not the feeling.\"
As you continue your flight, whenever the feeling returns, simply greet it: \"Hello again. You have a seat here, but you aren\'t flying the plane.\"
You managed your panic attack successfully. Every time you ride the wave, it gets easier.
It is getting better! Keep going.
Trust the process. It will pass.
You are doing great. Ride the wave.

You're thinking: "Just delay it? That can't possibly work." It feels too simple, but it's one of the most powerful tools in Metacognitive Therapy, the treatment that has been shown in research to reduce anxiety faster and more lastingly than traditional methods.

Your brain treats every scary thought as an urgent problem that must be solved immediately. In a plane, that's useless: there is nothing you can do about the wings or the engines right now. Keeping the worry running for hours only exhausts you.

The trick is to give the worry an official, specific time later - so your mind accepts that the job is safely scheduled and stops pressing the alarm button.

Do this right now:

Say to yourself (quietly or in your head):

"All worrying and what-if thoughts about the flight are now officially postponed until the very last minute of this flight, just before we land."
Whenever another scary thought appears, answer it with the exact same sentence:\n\n\"Thank you. Postponed until the final minute.\"
That\'s all. No fighting, no arguing, no reassuring yourself the plane is safe. Just postpone.
Most people notice the pressure drop within 30-60 seconds because the brain no longer believes the worry is needed right now.

And here\'s what almost always happens: when that final minute actually arrives hours later, you\'ll look up and realise the worry feels tiny - or you won\'t even remember what you were going to worry about.
Either way, you will have given yourself hours of calm instead of hours of torment.\n\nPostpone it. You haven\'t lost anything, and you\'ve just reclaimed the rest of your flight.

This technique is from Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). The \"riding the wave\" technique is based on a fundamental truth about all emotions: they are temporary and they follow a wave pattern. They rise, they peak, and they fall. Always. Without exception.\n\nThe wave metaphor isn\'t just poetic—it\'s neurologically accurate. Your nervous system literally cannot maintain peak anxiety indefinitely. It\'s biologically impossible.

Imagine you're at the beach. You see a wave coming. You have two choices:

Choice 1: Fight the wave. Brace yourself. Resist. What happens? The wave crashes into you, knocks you down, drags you under.

Choice 2: Ride the wave. You move with it rather than against it. What happens? The wave passes. You're still there. You're okay.

Anxiety works exactly the same way.

Find a comfortable position. Take a deep breath. Let's begin.

First, notice that anxiety is present. Where do you feel it in your body? Chest? Stomach? Hands?

Don't try to change it. Just notice where the wave is showing up in your body right now.

Say to yourself: "A wave of anxiety is here."

Now notice: Is the anxiety getting stronger? Is the wave building?

This is the wave rising. This is normal. This is what waves do.

Say to yourself: "The wave is rising. I'm going to ride it."

Breathe. Not to make it go away, but to anchor yourself as you ride.

Breathe in... breathe out.

You might feel like you're at the peak now. The anxiety might feel very strong.

Listen to me carefully: You are at the top of the wave. This is as big as it gets. The wave has nowhere to go but down.

Say to yourself: "This is the peak. I'm still here. I'm riding this."

Breathe with it. Feel the intensity. Notice it. Don't fight it.

Now, notice: Is the intensity the same? Or is it starting to ease, even just a little?

This is the wave falling. Your nervous system naturally returns to baseline. That's how bodies work.

Say to yourself: "The wave is falling. I'm coming down."

Just keep breathing. Keep riding. The wave is carrying you back down.

Notice now: Where is the anxiety?

The wave has passed. You rode it. You're still here.

Say to yourself: "I rode the wave. I'm okay."

This is the truth you just proved to yourself: Anxiety rises, peaks, and falls. Always. And you can ride it every single time.
Take a moment to recognize what just happened.\n\nYou felt anxiety. You didn\'t run from it. You didn\'t fight it. You acknowledged it. You named it. You rode it like a wave. And it passed.

Take a deep breath in... and out.

The wave came. You rode it. It passed. You're still here.

Remember this moment. Remember that you have this skill now. The next time anxiety rises, you'll know what to do.

When you feel anxiety rising during your flight: Name it: "A wave of anxiety is here."
Don't fight it: Let it rise. You're going to ride it.
Track the pattern: Notice when it's rising, peaking, falling.
Breathe with it.
Trust the process.

When you fight anxiety, you send your brain a message: \"This is dangerous.\" That triggers more anxiety. When you ride the wave, you send a different message: \"This is uncomfortable, but I can handle it. This will pass.\"\n\nFighting keeps you stuck in the wave. Riding lets you move through it.

Anxiety is a wave. It rises, it peaks, it falls.

You don't have to stop the wave. You don't have to calm the ocean. You just have to learn to surf.

And now you know how.
Find a comfortable position. Take a slow breath in through your nose… and out through your mouth. Let your shoulders drop.

Right now, you might be feeling anxious. That\'s okay. You don\'t need to push these feelings away.\n\nImagine you\'re flying toward a wall of dark clouds. From where you sit, they look heavy, almost solid. But up close, it\'s just mist. Your anxiety is like this cloud.
Breathe together. Each breath is like flying through the mist.\n\nBreathe in for four… hold… breathe out for six.

Notice your feelings. Tightness? Fluttering? Racing thoughts?

Don't run. Get curious. Move closer, like flying into the cloud. What is it really made of? A heartbeat? A physical sensation? A story your mind is telling?

As you look directly at each part, it becomes less solid.

The plane doesn't stop flying when it enters a cloud. The pilots don't panic. They know it's just mist.

You can let the anxiety be there, knowing it's just a cloud—no substance, no danger.

Breathe in… through the mist. Breathe out… emerging into clear sky.
Why does the whole plane vibrate and rattle before it even moves?

You're sitting there, the engines are still quiet, and suddenly the entire cabin starts shaking, rattling, and buzzing like something is loose or broken. It feels wrong and scary.

Here's exactly what's happening:

While you're waiting at the gate or taxiing, the pilots and the ground crew are doing last-second checks. The biggest shake usually comes when the pilots turn on the hydraulic pumps at full power and test the flight controls (ailerons, elevators, rudder).

Those big control surfaces on the wings and tail move quickly left-right and up-down. When they do, the hydraulic lines and actuators make the whole airframe vibrate and transmit the movement into the cabin. It's the same as when you test the steering wheel of a car hard left and right - the whole car shudders a little.

You might also hear a loud whining or barking sound under the floor. That's the PTU (Power Transfer Unit), a normal hydraulic system that makes a loud "dog barking" noise on many Airbus planes (and similar noises on Boeings). It only runs when one hydraulic system is at lower pressure - completely routine.

Sometimes the air-conditioning packs are switched from ground power to the engines or APU, and that makes the floor vibrate for a few seconds.

All of this happens before the plane even starts rolling and it is 100% normal. Pilots do it on every single flight. The plane is not falling apart - it's just waking up its muscles and making sure everything moves freely before the takeoff run. Nothing is loose, nothing is broken. It's the aviation version of stretching before a sprint.

Once the engines spool up and you start moving, most of that pre-flight rattling disappears.

You're perfectly safe - the plane is just saying "systems checked and ready."
That drop or dip right after takeoff - are we falling back down?

No, you're not falling. It feels exactly like the plane just lost all lift and is dropping, but it's actually a normal (and deliberate) maneuver that happens on almost every single takeoff.

Here's precisely what's going on:

As soon as the wheels leave the ground, the pilot pulls the nose up to a climb angle (usually around 10-15 degrees). That gives you the strong "pushing you back in your seat" feeling.

About 20-30 seconds later, at around 800-1,500 feet (245-460 m) above the runway, the pilot reduces engine power from full takeoff thrust to a lower "climb thrust." This is standard airline procedure to extend engine life and reduce noise over the airport area. The sudden drop in engine roar makes it feel like the power just disappeared.

At almost the same moment, the pilot lowers the nose slightly so the plane can accelerate to a safe climbing speed. That small pitch-down movement creates the unmistakable "elevator drop" or "sinking" sensation in your stomach.

On top of that, the huge flaps that were hanging down for takeoff start retracting, usually between 1,000-1,500 feet (305-460 m). When the first stage of flaps comes up, the wing temporarily loses a tiny bit of lift, which adds to the sinking feeling.

All of this happens in the first minute or so after takeoff. It feels dramatic because you're still relatively low and your body isn't used to it, but the plane is climbing the entire time. The altimeter is going up, not down.

Pilots do this on every flight, every day, millions of times a year. It's not an emergency, it's not a mistake, and the plane is nowhere near stalling or falling.

It's just the normal "clean-up" phase after takeoff: reduce power -> lower the nose a little -> retract flaps -> settle into a steady climb.

Next time you feel that dip, remind yourself: "That's just the pilot shifting gears."

It always passes in seconds, and then the ride smooths out. You're climbing safely the whole time.
